newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish PM to tackle tough issues with Russia.
newsitem.headline: Polish PM to tackle tough issues with Russia.

text.p: Poland's Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz said ahead of a visit to Moscow on Tuesday that he would not avoid tough issues such as European security during talks with Russian leaders.
"I also think this will be a good chance to talk about difficult issues, among others security matters," he said.
He also told reporters he would sign agreements, including one settling mutual trade debts left from the communist era, and would discuss plans to prepare an easing of bilateral trade.
Cimoszewicz said he expected the Russians to stress European security while he was most concerned with the problem of spreading international crime.
The main irritant in bilateral ties is Russia's opposition to Poland's plans to become a full member of NATO quickly.
Moscow denounces the western alliance's enlargement as a potential threat, while some Polish officials suspect Russia aims to retain a traditional sphere of influence embracing Poland.
Cimoszewicz said NATO's enlargement was not up to Poland and Russia to decide but he wanted to hear Russia's objections.
"In my view there are no serious substantial counter arguments," he said.
Poland, which escaped Soviet domination in 1989, is anxious that Russian pressure should not persuade NATO states to water down guarantees which Warsaw seeks from membership.

"I would like the main message of this visit reaching the ordinary Russian to be that Poland wants good relations with Russia, we want to cooperate, but that we don't forget we also have rights," he said.
Russia has suggested a bilateral free-trade zone but Poland has said it cannot yet agree because of effects on other trade partners, especially the European Union which it wants to join.
Poland is, however, interested in relaxing barriers to trade with Russia where possible.

Cimoszewicz will meet Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and other top officials on Wednesday, visit St Petersburg for business-related talks and go on to Tatarstan to discuss trade and oil imports from the autonomous republic.
He is not scheduled to meet President Boris Yeltsin, recovering from heart surgery but will see Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais during the trip ending on Friday.
His trip follows a visit by Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski to Moscow in April.
